1.pericope_label: The law binds a man only while he lives, as a wife is bound only while her husband lives

schools.summary: Open by naming the quarrel that runs through the chapter, that few chapters have been the subject of more decidedly different interpretations and that it is still discussed whether the apostle refers to his own experience before conversion or to the conflicts of a mind already renewed, while the main design is not in doubt — to show the insufficiency of the law to produce peace of mind in a troubled sinner; treat the illustration as simple and blame the expositors, since had it been kept in mind that the point is merely that death dissolves the relations which make law binding in life, it would have saved much perplexity and many wild vagaries about men being the wife and the law the former husband, such expositions being enough to make us mourn over the puerile interpretations even wise men give the Bible; state the defect of the illustration precisely instead, that the law is represented by the husband though the apostle means the Christian dies to the law and not the law to the Christian, so the proposition must be taken abstractly; explain how the Gentile half of the church would know the law well enough for the argument to bite, from intercourse with the Jewish members and from hearing the Old Testament read in the synagogues; and keep the address wider still, since the Romans, whether Jews or Gentiles, knew the principle of law, identifying the word for the married woman as a late compound meaning under a husband and the verb of her release as a perfect, so that she stands free.

Explain why the argument had to be resumed: the question of the law's abrogation had been settled briefly already, but it was difficult and bred further questions, so the apostle now shows at length how the law is abrogated with regard to us and what good is thereby done, since while it holds us separated from Christ and bound to itself it can do nothing but condemn us; and make the mismatch in the illustration deliberate, since the apostle might have completed the comparison by saying the law is dead to us, but rather than offend the Jews by the asperity of the expression he turned aside and said that we are dead to the law. Elsewhere take the address for the Jewish converts at Rome, and think the word brethren chosen to soften their resentment, since they were zealous of the law and would be displeased by what had just been said.

Agree that the appeal is chiefly to Jews and add the motive, that the apostle is weaning them from their fondness for the Mosaic law, giving the anxiety behind that fondness — they rested in the law as sufficient for justification, and to renounce it might appear a renunciation of their allegiance to God; dissolve the difficulty of the illustration altogether, since the law is spoken of by a common figure as a person, to which life and death are ascribed as to a husband, the apostle speaking indifferently of the law being dead to us or we to it, the sense being the same; and turn the whole to use, that this change argues no disloyalty to the Maker, since the law of ordinances was determined to cease and a believer is as free to receive the gospel as such a woman would be to marry again.
Guard the charge of adultery: the law calls her an adulteress not who is united to another after her husband's death but who joins herself to another while he is yet alive.

Set out what the deliverance covers: we are freed from the power of the law that curses and condemns, the sentence against us being vacated by the death of Christ, and also from that power of the law which irritates and provokes the sin dwelling in us.

debates: Whether the chapter describes the apostle before or after his conversion.
Whom the argument is addressed to, and how much law they knew.
In what respect the illustration of the widow fails to fit.
Whether it is the law that dies to us or we that die to the law.
outliers: Barnes names the great interpretative division of the chapter in his first sentence, and defers deciding it.
Barnes blames the expositors for the difficulty; Ellicott locates it in the illustration; Calvin makes it a deliberate concession to Jewish readers.
Wesley denies there is a difficulty at all, since the law being dead to us and we to it come to the same thing.
Ellicott alone explains how Gentile converts came to know the Mosaic law.
Henry alone distinguishes deliverance from the law that condemns and from the law that provokes.

4.pericope_label: Dead to the law by the body of Christ, that we should serve in newness of spirit

schools.summary: Insist that the point is incontestable from what follows, that it is the moral law and not the ceremonial spoken of here, since the apostle quotes a moral commandment in the next verse and says that by it sin slew him, which could not be said of the ceremonial law; say that as long as the literal teaching of the law rules unconnected with the Spirit of Christ the wantonness of the flesh is not restrained but breaks out and prevails, so that those under it attain nothing but this, that their ears are struck by an external sound without fruit or effect — whence the zealots of the law act unreasonably in wishing to detain the faithful under its dominion, since bondage to the law produces sin only, and if the former leads to death then freedom must tend to righteousness and life. Elsewhere enumerate the releases — from the ministration by Moses, from the law as a covenant of works, from its rigorous exaction, from its curse, and from its being an irritant to sin — while adding the proviso that we are not freed from obedience to it as it is in the hands of Christ.

Read the passage as a transfer from one constitution to another in which the merely literal rites, ceremonies and sacrifices are done away, so that we now know the spiritual import of all the Mosaic precepts; give the plainest account of what the yoke was, that it sentenced every transgressor to perdition and provided no pardon even for the penitent and no sanctification for those weary of their inbred corruptions; and gloss the working in the members as spreading themselves over the whole man, and the sins by the law as accidentally occasioned or irritated by it.

Take in the flesh to mean under the polity of the law, understanding by the flesh the legislative ordinances concerning foods and drinks and leprosy and the like; notice the delicacy of the apostle's phrasing and give the reason, that he still continues in his cautious mode of expression and says not that the law is made to cease but that we are made to cease from the law; explain how the release was effected, that being subjects of the law we came to baptism, and dying with Christ and with him rising again we were united to our Lawgiver, so that we no longer need the polity of the law; and distinguish carefully that the apostle says not that the passions were in the law but by the law, for the law does not itself bring about sin but condemns it, sin using for evil what was good — neither do our members bring about sin, but only by our members has the inclination of the soul to the worse brought its operations into effect.

List what Christians are freed from — the law as a means of justification, as a source of sanctification, and as a bondage — and then stop, since it does not mean they are freed from it as a rule of duty; report the variation in the manuscripts, some reading as though the law were dead and others as though we were, noting that the majority favour the latter and that the connexion requires it; trace the history of the error instead, since the translators seem to have followed a reading found in no manuscript at all, which arose from a mistake of two editors in interpreting a patristic comment, the true text running that we were delivered from the law, having died to that wherein we were held; say that in the act of our baptism, which united us to Christ, we obtained release from our old tyrant the law, and that the clause about serving expresses result rather than purpose, our release from one master implying an engagement to another; and put the conclusion plainly, that the death to the letter of the law has set us free to the new life in Christ.

debates: Whether the law we are freed from is the moral law or the ceremonial.
What the deliverance does not release us from.
Whether the text says the law died or that we died.
At what point the release from the law took effect.
Whether the law itself produces the sin it occasions.
outliers: Calvin argues from the next verse that only the moral law can be meant; Clarke and Theodoret read the passage of the ceremonial system.
Barnes and Gill independently add the same proviso, that freedom from the law is not freedom from it as a rule of duty.
Ellicott traces the received reading to an editorial misunderstanding of Chrysostom; Barnes reaches the same text by counting manuscripts.
Theodoret notices the same tactful avoidance of saying the law is dead that Calvin had remarked on at the opening of the chapter.
Ellicott and Theodoret both locate the release from the law in baptism.

7.pericope_label: Is the law sin? — I had not known lust except the law had said, Thou shalt not covet

schools.summary: Answer flatly the question the chapter is famous for: this is a kind of digression in which the apostle, to show the weakness of the law most vividly, changes the person and speaks as of himself about the misery of a man under the law, a thing he frequently does when not speaking of his own person but assuming another character — the character assumed being that of a man first ignorant of the law, then under it, sincerely but ineffectually striving to serve God, so that to have spoken this of himself or of any true believer would have been foreign to the whole scope of the discourse and indeed contrary to it; add that sin before the law was neither so apparent nor so active, and that the speaker was under no apprehension of danger from it; and elsewhere let the personification stand at full height, sin being represented as a murderer watching for life and snatching at every means to carry his fell purpose into effect, so that the miserable sinner has a murderer within him, while reviewing the renderings proposed for the phrase about occasion and rejecting one as having no authority beyond its etymology, and holding that the pointing is wrong, the comma belonging after occasion and not after commandment.

Resist the autobiographical reading, wondering what could have come into the minds of interpreters to render the passage in a past tense as though the apostle were speaking of himself, when his purpose was plainly to begin with a general proposition and only then explain it by his own example; reduce the whole to a sentence, that the knowledge of sin without the law is buried; and settle what the commandment is, either the whole moral law or that particular precept against coveting, which the Jews say comprehends all.

De-personify sin carefully: it means here not a real entity, not a physical subsistence, not something independent of the mind having a separate existence and lodged in the soul, but the corrupt passions and inclinations of the mind itself — as we say that lust burns and ambition rages and envy corrodes, without supposing any of them independent subsistences — adding that perhaps nowhere has the apostle shown more consummate knowledge of the human heart than here; say that the Greek for taking occasion implies a base of operations, an advanced post occupied as the starting-point and rendezvous for further advances, and that sin cannot act on a man without the co-operation of law; prefer elsewhere a starting-place from which to rush into acts of sin, excuses for doing what men want to do, illustrating it from the present century, since drinking men use the prohibition laws as occasions for violating them; raise the question of construction, whether by the commandment attaches to the taking of occasion or to the working in me, the sense coming to much the same either way though there are reasons of some force for the second; and make dead exact, meaning inactive and not non-existent, sin being in reality present in a dormant state.

State what the objection is that all this answers, and why it had to be met: having said so much about the influence of the law as a covenant upon the dominion of sin, the apostle might easily be misinterpreted as reflecting on the law, and so shows from his own experience its excellency and usefulness — not as a covenant but as a guide — for laws are as the lawmakers are, and God being holy, just and good, his law must needs be so; it commands holiness and encourages it, it is consonant to the rules of equity and right reason, and it was given for the good of mankind and the conservation of peace and order in the world.

Use the military figure, that sin made the imposition of the law a means for battle and beat down the weaker powers of judgment; put the principle plainly, that where there is no law pointing out what should be done and forbidding what should not, sin has no place; and name the apologetic motive that governs the passage, since having said that sins were increased by the imposition of the law the apostle sets out its manner in every way he can, lest anyone should suppose that the law had been their cause.

debates: Whether the apostle speaks of himself here or assumes another character.
Whether sin in this chapter is an agent or a way of speaking about the mind.
What the phrase rendered taking occasion conveys.
Whether by the commandment governs the taking of occasion or the working of desire.
In what sense sin was dead before the commandment came.
outliers: Wesley denies outright that the speaker can be the apostle or any believer; Calvin resists the autobiographical reading on grammatical grounds instead.
Barnes insists sin is no independent subsistence; Clarke makes it a murderer lodged within the man.
Ellicott and Theodoret independently read the key phrase as a military metaphor.
Robertson illustrates the occasion of sin from the prohibition laws of his own day.
Robertson alone insists that dead here means dormant rather than absent.

9.pericope_label: I was alive without the law once — the commandment ordained to life I found to be unto death — wherefore the law is holy

schools.summary: Refuse both of the historical identifications on offer and hold the speaker to be neither Adam nor Israel before Sinai: Adam never lived without law, having the law of nature written on his heart and a positive precept respecting the forbidden fruit given him as a trial of obedience, and in him sin could not be said to revive, since it never lived before; nor were the sons of Abraham without law, having besides the law of nature the laws of circumcision and sacrifice and the several duties of religion. Give the life a psychological account instead: the absence of the law was the reason the man was alive, that is, being inflated with a conceit as to his own righteousness he claimed life to himself while he was yet dead, so that the death of sin is the life of man and the life of sin the death of man. Narrow what the commandment was ordained to, namely a continuance of immortal life to Adam on perfect obedience and a quiet possession of Canaan to Israel, but never eternal life, which is the free gift of God without respect to works. Call the deadly wound incidental, as an incurable disease is exasperated by a healing remedy, an inseparable incident so that the law is elsewhere the ministration of death, yet not in its own nature hurtful. Shift the deceiving from the thing to our knowledge of it, since we are led out of the way only in the sense that sin is made evident by the law and sinners who before went on heedlessly now loathe themselves. And read the three epithets as a point-by-point antithesis to the character of sin, sin working depraved lusts where the law is holy, sin acting the traitor where the law is plain dealing, sin leading to death where the law leads to happiness.

Take the passage as the apostle’s own past experience, since there seems to be no doubt of it, while insisting that in it he speaks the sentiment of all who are unconverted and depending on their own righteousness; explain the life as a certain kind of peace, free from the convictions of conscience and the agitations of alarm, aiming at external conformity and unacquainted with the spiritual claims of the law. Press the tense of revived, which does not mean that sin came to life but that it came to life again, sin lurking in the heart from the first but dormant until the Commandment comes. Argue the goodness of the law in steps: it is good and produces no evil; on a being perfectly holy and perfectly obedient it would produce life and happiness only; for that it was ordained and is adapted; but man is a sinner, and on him the same law crosses inclination and brings woe. Stop on the verb rendered I found, which is passive and not active, so that the sense is that it turned out so for me. Gloss the beguiling as a leading away from the right way, urging the sinner on headlong and without deliberation, and illustrate it from Solomon’s ox going to the slaughter; render the slaying bluntly as killed me off, made a clean job of it, with sin personified as the tempter. Note that the wherefore draws its conclusion not from the verse immediately preceding but from the whole of the last five verses, answering the question raised at the opening of the paragraph, and end by observing that the modern revolt against law needs these words.

Follow Whitby in referring the words to the seed of Abraham, alive before the law was given because not obnoxious to death for that to which the law had not yet threatened death, so that when the commandment came forbidding it under that penalty, sin gained strength to draw to sin and to condemn to death; describe sin throughout as an armed and flagrant adversary that wars against the mind, besets us, brings us into bondage and entices us. Say in the first person what the earlier life felt like: I had much life, wisdom, virtue, strength, so I thought; but when the commandment came in its spiritual meaning to the heart with the power of God, my inbred sin took fire and all my virtue and strength died away. Hold that the commandment was originally intended by God as a grand means of preserving and increasing spiritual life, and that it presented the duty and laid down the penalty without affording any strength to resist sin. Hear Eve behind the deceiving, the apostle using the very expression the Septuagint gives her, and note that the verb for slaying also means to make wretched, so that the sinner lives a dying life or a living death. And read the conclusion as a soothing of his countrymen: nothing improper or imperfect is intimated in the law as a rule of life, and it is because it is holy, just and good that it condemns transgressors to death.

Refer the whole of it to Adam before his transgression, who had no fear of death until the commandment respecting the trees was imposed, whereupon the devil came to the woman in the serpent and uttered his deceitful speeches, and she being enticed and beholding the beauty of the fruit was overcome by desire and broke the commandment, Adam sharing both the food and the sentence. Vindicate the law in every way while proving the evil of sin: the commandment was the minister of life, but the turning aside to evil begot death, and the word found is chosen precisely to show that the intention of the law and the end brought about by sin were widely different things. Pass over the repetition briefly, since the same thing had been said before in different words. Then split the two terms of the conclusion, taking the law for the Mosaic and the commandment for that given to Adam, and account for the greater praise heaped on the latter by the greater censure it commonly meets, since they who live in idle ease and will not undergo the labours of virtue cry out even against God for imposing it, asking how He can be God if He did not foresee the transgression, and charging Him with its cause if He did — whereas the power of discriminating between good and its opposite belongs to those gifted with reason, the irrational creatures having no such faculty and no sense of sin.

debates: Whether the speaker is Adam, Israel before Sinai, or the apostle himself.
In what sense a man can be said to have been alive before the law reached him.
What the commandment was ordained to give, and to whom.
Whether the deceiving is a real seduction or a disclosure of an existing state.
Whether the law and the commandment are two things or one.
outliers: Gill states and rejects the Adam reading that Theodoret holds and the pre-Sinai reading that Clarke holds, all three within the same catena.
Calvin makes the deceiving epistemic rather than actual, against Barnes, Clarke and Robertson together.
Theodoret alone distinguishes the Mosaic law from the commandment given to Adam.
Gill denies that the commandment was ever ordained to eternal life, where Barnes and Calvin let the promise stand and blame the failure on the man.
Robertson borrows Denney’s phrase for the lost paradise in the infancy of men and Shedd’s for a seeming life.

13.pericope_label: Was then that which is good made death unto me? — that sin by the commandment might become exceeding sinful

schools.summary: Treat the verse as an objection started and taken out of the mouth of another person, and show that it proceeds on a mistake of the apostle’s meaning: he had said that he died when the commandment came and that he found it to be unto death, but he gave no intimation that the law was the cause of his death; at most it was an occasion, and that occasion was not given by the law but taken by sin, which deceived him and slew him. Deny that it is any objection to the goodness of the law that it is a ministration of condemnation and death to sinners, and rest on the maxim that a law which does not condemn is no law at all, a law without a sanction being no law. State also what had until now remained doubtful, namely how it could be that nothing but death was gained from so singular a gift of God, and answer by a distinction: it is through our wickedness that the law is turned to our destruction and contrary to its own character, but it is not the cause of death in such a sense that death is to be imputed to it. Then handle the harder parallel where the law is called the ministration of death, arguing that the phrase represents not the real character of the law but the false opinion of opponents — and let the printed note contradict that argument in the next breath, saying that this can hardly be admitted since the apostle there evidently states a fact, the fact being that the law proved to be the ministration of death, though it proved so through something other than itself.

Put the objection generally, whether that which is admitted to be good and pure can be changed into evil and whether that which tends to life can be made death to a man, and answer that the fault was not in the law but in the man and his sinful propensities. Read the purpose clause as development rather than manufacture: sin was to show its true nature and no longer lie dormant in the mind, the law of God being applied to a man’s conscience so that he may see how deep and desperate his depravity is, since no man knows his own heart until the law thus crosses his path and shows him what he is. Handle the intensive phrase as one of the apostle’s strongest, meaning in an extensive degree and to the utmost possible extent, and note that the English hyperbole is simply the Greek word carried over. Parse the clause as a final clause with sin working death as an incidental result, and conclude bluntly that the sinfulness of sin is revealed in its violations of God’s law, that the excesses of sin reveal its real nature, and that only then do some people get their eyes opened. Add the reversal at the end: this short-lived dominion was no triumph for sin after all, since the very law it took for its stay turned round upon it and condemned it, sin no longer remaining covert and unrecognised but coming out in its true colours.

Make the objection a Jew’s and the passage a dispute with a countryman, who asks whether the law may be allowed good and still be called the cause of our death, and answer by no means: it is not the law that is the cause of your death but sin, which subjected us to death by a law justly threatening sin with death. Draw the practical consequence, that a man cannot have a true notion of sin except by means of the law of God, that one design of the law was to show the abominable and destructive nature of sin as well as to be a rule of life, and that it would be almost impossible for a man to have that just notion of the demerit of sin which produces repentance, or to see the nature and necessity of the death of Christ, if the law were not applied to his conscience by the light of the Holy Spirit. Keep the experimental note as well: that which is good was not made the cause of evil, nor of death which is the greatest of evils, but inbred sin, driving furiously in spite of the commandment, became exceeding sinful, the guilt of it being greatly aggravated.

Deny the suggestion according to your wont and lay the cause of these evils on sin; then blame the obscurity of the verse on the extreme brevity used, and supply the argument at length: by that which is good, to wit the law and commandment, sin is made apparent as being bad and evil, and it is made apparent by its working unto death, for from the fruit I know the tree, and seeing death I hate its parent — and of all this the law is the teacher, so that it is not the law which thus instructs that is evil but sin, which brings death. Add that though nature points out sin, its excessive turpitude the law has more clearly manifested. And name what the others leave unnamed, that the author of sin is the inclination of our own free will to the worse.

debates: Whose objection this is — a Jew’s, a general objector’s, or a device of the apostle’s own.
Whether the law is the cause of death or only the occasion of it.
What the clause about sin appearing sin is meant to accomplish.
Whether the ministration of death states the law’s character or an opponent’s opinion of it.
What makes a man the author of his own sin.
outliers: Gill answers the objection with the maxim that a law without a sanction is no law.
The printed Calvin contradicts itself within a few lines, the dissent being the editor’s hand rather than Calvin’s, with nothing in the catena to mark the change.
Theodoret alone grounds the argument in free will, making the inclination of our own will to the worse the author of sin.
Ellicott reverses the figure: the law sin took for its base turned round and condemned it.
Robertson observes that the English hyperbole is the Greek word itself.

14.pericope_label: For we know that the law is spiritual; but I am carnal, sold under sin

schools.summary: Come down for the post-conversion reading of the whole remainder of the chapter and give the reasons in order: it is the most obvious meaning, the one plain men will take who have no theory to support and who understand language in its usual sense; it agrees with the design of the argument, which is to show that the law is not adapted to produce sanctification and peace, so that referring it to the period before conversion would repeat what is already settled and leave a whole field open in which the law might still be thought to sanctify; and the expressions later in the chapter cannot be understood of an impenitent sinner. Decline to argue that the law is spiritual, since Christians all know it to be divinely given and inspired, and set against it the man who, though capable of communion with God, is dominated by the part of his nature that is entirely earthly and sensual, a slave as much as if he had been sold in the auction mart. Give the adjective its shortest gloss, spirit-caused and spirit-given and like the Holy Spirit; make the word for carnal more emphatic than the usual form, a creature of flesh; and read the participle as a state of completion, sin having closed the mortgage and now owning its slave.

Take the passage as a demonstration of the insufficiency of the law in opposition to the gospel, the one giving knowledge of sin and the other its cure, and deny outright that by the word I the apostle can mean himself or any Christian believer, since if the contrary could be proved the argument would demonstrate the insufficiency of the gospel as well as the law; hold instead that he is personating a Jew under the law and without the gospel, or describing his own state when he was such. Say how the other opinion looks: it is difficult to conceive how it could have crept into the Church, and it has most pitifully and shamefully not only lowered the standard of Christianity but destroyed its influence and disgraced its character. Deny too that the law is a system of external rites or even merely a rule of moral action, since it is a spiritual system reaching to the most hidden purposes and dispositions of the heart and condemning without hope of reprieve whatever is contrary to eternal rectitude. And elsewhere refuse the flat alternative, treating the passage as interweaving the whole process of a man reasoning, groaning, striving and escaping from the legal to the evangelical state, with sold under sin meaning totally enslaved, as slaves bought with money were absolutely at their master’s disposal.

Ground the word spiritual in its origin and its reach: the law comes from the Spirit of God and reaches to the spirit of man, requiring truth in the inward parts, spiritual service and obedience, a serving of it with our minds and a loving of God with all our hearts as well as the outward acts of religion, and it cannot be truly obeyed without the assistance of the Spirit of God — from which it follows that it can never be the cause of sin or death. Begin here to compare the law more closely with what man is, so that it may be understood whence the evil of death proceeds, and set before us an example in a regenerate man, in whom the remnants of the flesh are wholly contrary to the law of the Lord while the spirit would gladly obey it. Reject the narrower exposition which makes spiritual mean only that the law binds the feelings of the heart and not merely the hands and feet: the word stands here by way of contrast to carnal, so that as flesh means what is sinful and corrupt, spiritual imports what is holy and just and good, and under the term flesh is included whatever men bring from the womb. Since in human things there is no greater discord than between spirit and flesh, ask what agreement there can be between the natural man and the law, and answer, the same as between darkness and light.

State the deadlock as a deadlock and do not resolve it: this is a description of the conflict between grace and corruption in the heart, and it is applicable two ways, to the struggles of a convinced but still unregenerate soul and to those of a renewed and sanctified soul still in a state of imperfection, and a great controversy there is which of these is meant. So far does the evil prevail here, when he speaks of one sold under sin, doing what he would not and not performing what is good, that it seems difficult to apply the words to the regenerate, who are described as walking not after the flesh but after the Spirit; and yet so far does the good prevail, in hating sin, consenting to the law, delighting in it and serving the law of God with the mind, that it is more difficult still to apply them to the unregenerate, who are dead in trespasses and sins. Then expound it both ways in turn, first of the man who knows his Lord’s will and approves the things that are more excellent, being instructed out of the law, and yet lives in constant breach of it, having that within him which witnesses against the sin he commits and yet continuing a slave to his reigning lusts.

Observe that the apostle is still clearing the law of suspicion, and that he does it not by acquittal only but by encircling it with the utmost praise, and that he lays it down not as a concession of his own but as a universal judgment, since we know is an allowed and self-evident thing. Explain what the praise amounts to: by calling the law spiritual he shows it to be a teacher of virtue and hostile to vice, leading off from sin of every kind by frightening, admonishing, chastening, correcting and recommending every kind of virtue; and if the teacher was so admirable, ask whence sin was produced, and answer, from the listlessness of its disciples. Elsewhere crown the law with the same praise on the ground that it was written by divine inspiration, blessed Moses being a partaker of that grace when he indited it. Refer the carnal man to one who lived before the coming of grace, beset by his passions and not yet in receipt of the spiritual help offered in the new covenant; and read sold under sin by the prophet’s reproach that for your iniquities have you sold yourselves, so that the man delivered himself up to sin and sold himself to it.

debates: Whether the man described from here to the end of the chapter is regenerate or not.
Whether the question can be settled at all, or must be expounded both ways.
What calling the law spiritual asserts about it.
Who did the selling in the phrase sold under sin.
Why sin arose if the law that taught against it was so good.
outliers: Clarke calls the regenerate reading a shameful lowering of the standard of Christianity; Calvin and Barnes hold it.
Henry declines to decide and expounds the passage twice over, once each way.
Wesley refuses the alternative altogether and makes the passage a process of escape from the legal to the evangelical state.
Calvin argues against an unnamed group of interpreters who make spiritual mean only inwardness.
Chrysostom lays the origin of sin at the listlessness of the law’s disciples rather than at any fault in the teacher.
Theodoret makes the man his own seller, reading the phrase through Isaiah’s reproach.

15.pericope_label: That which I do I allow not — if I do that which I would not, I consent unto the law that it is good — it is no more I that do it, but sin that dwelleth in me

schools.summary: Keep the English rendering of the first clause but justify it, since the Greek is I know not and the verb for knowing is sometimes used in the sense of approving; then read the whole as the prevailing bent of the inclinations set against what is actually done, the strong native propensity to sin persisting even under the restraining influence of the gospel. Elsewhere take the same clause flatly as blind action, without conscious direction of the will, the higher part of a man which should preside over his actions kept down by the lower physical nature; and note that three distinct words for doing occur in the passage, the one used here and at the disowning being the strongest, a deliberate action thoroughly carried out, while the other two differ as do and practise, the one of single and the other of habitual acts. Make the failure a failure of perception, a not recognising the thing in its true nature because the spiritual faculties are dulled, and let the phrase about being sold under sin turn the scale for the period before conversion, since this is the unregenerate man’s experience surviving in memory into regenerate days and read with regenerate eyes. Turn the consent into a test of piety, because the struggle itself proves that the evil is not loved and the law that condemns it is, so that nothing can be a more decisive evidence than a long-continued and painful struggle against evil desire; and add that the very wish to do the opposite of what is done is an acceptance of God’s law as good. Find a real dualism in the soul and refuse to be identified with the lower self that is enthralled by sin, while denying that the paradox removes moral responsibility, since to be saved from sin a man must at the same time own it and disown it; and describe the tenant as sin dwelling in the mind as in its home, not yet wholly dislodged.

Narrow what is being confessed: not a notorious crime committed and repeated, nor a sinful course of life, since the man was externally moral before his conversion and afterwards walked by grace in righteousness, but internal lusts, the workings of corruption in the heart, which are real actions of the mind, together with the frailties and infirmities of life. Draw the inferences step by step, that what was done was contrary to the law yet neither willed nor allowed but hated, and that therefore it was not the man as spiritual and born again who did it. Come at this point to the particular case of a man already regenerated, and press the following verse as proof that none but the godly are in view, since the apostle denies that he is wholly possessed by sin and declares himself exempt from its bondage, sin dwelling only in some part of his soul while with an earnest feeling of heart he strives after the righteousness of God. Distinguish the consent sharply from that of the ungodly who have said that they see the better things and approve them while following the worse, for those act under constraint when they subscribe to the righteousness of God, their will being wholly alienated from it, whereas the godly man consents to the law with the real and most cheerful desire of his heart. And deny that the disowning is a self-excusing plea, as with the many triflers who think they have a sufficient defence for all their wickedness when they cast the blame on the flesh; it is instead a declaration of how far a man dissents from his own flesh in his spiritual feeling.

Take the first clause as a general assertion about the employment of a man in the state just called carnal and sold under sin, and press the verb, which means a work the agent continues to perform until it is finished, the same word used of working out one’s own salvation; so that what the man is continually labouring at he does not acknowledge to be right or just or holy or profitable, being a slave under the absolute control of a tyrannical master, hating the service but obliged to work his master’s will. Ask who, without blaspheming, can assert that this is spoken of a man in whom the Spirit of the Lord dwells. Read the consent simply: knowing that the law condemns the thing and that it must therefore be evil, the man acknowledges by that very circumstance that the law is good, and the single word good here implies all three of the epithets used before. Then describe the tenant of the disowning as a principle in the unregenerate man stronger than reason itself, not properly of the essence of the soul but acting in it as its lord or as a tyrant, darkening the understanding and perverting the judgment — inbred and indwelling sin, the seed of the serpent, for which there is condemnation in the law but no cure.

Supply the psychology of the first clause: he who is overcome by pleasure, and he also who is intoxicated by the passion of anger, has no clear perception of sin, but receives a knowledge of the evil only after the passion has subsided. Call it the perfection of the law to point out what is evil and implant a hatred of it in the soul, and insist that the words about doing what one hates denote not compulsion but weakness, since we sin not because driven by necessity or force but because, being beguiled by pleasure, we fall into the very things we cannot but hate and denounce as wicked. Say that the hatred of sin was itself received from the law, so that the man bears the law testimony and acknowledges its excellence. Guard the same ground against a perverse interpretation of the clause about doing what one would not: the soul committed no sin before it came into this world but came in sinless, and we now sin of our free will — remember Him who said that if ye be willing and hearken unto Me ye shall eat the good things of the land, but if ye be not willing the sword shall devour you, and the reproach of the fruitful vine turned to bitterness. And explain the indwelling at length from the body, which after the transgression became mortal and received passions and appetites, without which our present state could not be carried on, since desire provides food and children and agriculture and the arts, and even qualifies us to bear the difficulties that attend virtue and works the divine love within us.

debates: What the clause rendered I allow not actually denies — approval, knowledge, or clear perception.
Whether the doing described is deliberate performance or habitual practice.
Whether the speaker of these verses is regenerate.
What the consent to the law proves about the man who gives it.
How far a man may disown the sin that dwells in him.
outliers: Ellicott distinguishes three separate verbs for doing in the passage; the others render them alike.
Robertson takes sold under sin as decisive for the pre-conversion reading, where Calvin takes the disowning of verse 17 as decisive against it.
Calvin sets the believer’s consent against the pagan maxim of seeing the better and following the worse.
Cyril reads the verse as a threat to free will and answers it rather than expounding it.
Theodoret leaves the argument to defend the appetites themselves as necessary to food, family, agriculture and the arts.
The editorial matter printed with Calvin catalogues rival schemes he never mentions — a law state, a Jew between Abraham and Sinai, a fiction about proselytes.

18.pericope_label: In my flesh dwelleth no good thing — to will is present with me, but how to perform that which is good I find not

schools.summary: Read the qualifying phrase as an illustration of the indwelling just asserted, and press it as evidence for the larger question: the careful saying in my flesh implies that there was in the man at that time something right and acceptable with God which did not pertain to him by nature. Find in the denial of any good thing the strongest possible expression of total depravity, spoken by the apostle of himself, and turn it into a means of self-examination, asking whether we have such a view of our own native character as to say the same. Take the phrase elsewhere more guardedly as meaning not absolutely good, and deny that it is a complete view of man even in his unregenerate state, since the wishing belongs to the better self and only the doing to the lower. Acknowledge the following verse as substantially a repetition, and explain the repetition as a mark of how full the mind is of the subject and how inclined to place it in every variety of form even at the hazard of repeating; and acknowledge the verse after it as a repetition too. Then guard the disowning against abuse, since the real self no longer performs the thing and yet responsibility and guilt remain, the struggle going on.

Say that no good dwelt in the man by nature, the qualifying words meaning so far as it regards myself; then subjoin a modification, lest the grace of God which also dwelt in him, though no part of his flesh, be slighted — and take this as confirming that the faithful and not men in general are in view, since the faithful are divided into two parts, the relics of the flesh and grace, and the modification would have no purpose unless some part were exempt from depravity and therefore not flesh. Under the term flesh include all that human nature is, everything in man except the sanctification of the Spirit, and under the opposed term the part of the soul which the Spirit has re-formed and purified so that God’s image shines in it. State the want of power plainly, that the man had a will to what was good but no strength of his own to perform, and so often did what he would not. Draw the hard consequence from the generality of the description, that since the whole course of the godly life is delineated and not merely some of their faults, their best works are always stained with blots of sin and no reward can be hoped unless God pardons them; add that had the pure integrity of our nature remained the law would not have brought death upon us, and that to restore health is the work of our heavenly Physician. And guard the last inference against misuse: it is drawn not to excuse the man from blame in sinning but to trace the lusts of his heart and the sins of his life to their fountain in the corruption of his nature, and to ascribe them neither to the law nor to the new man but to the sin dwelling in him.

Gloss the flesh in one line as the whole man as he is by nature. Then say from experience that in an unregenerate man there is no good, no principle by which the soul can be brought into the light or restored to purity, fleshly appetites alone prevailing so that the brute runs away with the man — but immediately qualify it, since though the whole soul suffered indescribably by the Fall some faculties suffered less, or rather received larger measures of supernatural light, their concurrence being necessary to salvation; for even the most unconcerned about spiritual things have understanding, judgment, reason and will, by means of which scoffers at revelation have become eminent metaphysicians, physicians, mathematicians, astronomers and chemists. Take this to its conclusion at the next verse: here is decisive proof that the will is on the side of God and truth and opposed to evil, being found almost uniformly on God’s side while the whole sensual system is against him; it is not the will that leads men astray but the corrupt passions which oppose and oppress it; and this almost only friend to God in the human soul has been slandered as God’s worst enemy, and that by men who had the seventh chapter to the Romans before their eyes. Describe the resulting state as a perpetual self-contradiction, two principles contending for the mastery, reason on which the light of God shines and passion in which the principle of sin works; and recall that this contradiction led some ancient philosophers to imagine that a man has two souls, telling the story from Xenophon of the Persian nobleman who confessed to Cyrus that he must have two souls, since one could not at the same time pant after vice and virtue.

Trace the whole disability to the passions: their dominion was introduced by the mortality of the body and has been strengthened by the indolence of the mind. Then divide the verse accordingly, since as regards a willingness towards that which is good the man has received it from the teaching of the law, but as regards action he is impotent for want of further help. Let the following verses stand almost bare, repeating the words with little comment, since the same thing has already been said.

Make the experience a mark of grace rather than a problem to be solved: the more pure and holy the heart is, the quicker will be its feeling of the sin that remains in it, since the believer sees more of the beauty of holiness and the excellence of the law, and his earnest desires to obey increase as he grows in grace. Yet the whole good on which his will is fully bent he does not do, sin ever springing up through remaining corruption, so that he often does evil against the fixed determination of his will, and the motions of sin within grieve him. Observe that the opposition runs both ways, for if the striving of the flesh against the Spirit means he cannot do as the Spirit suggests, the effectual opposition of the Spirit equally means he cannot do what the flesh prompts. And set the whole against a contrary case: those who make themselves easy about the inward motions of the flesh prompting them to evil, and who against the light and warning of conscience go on even in outward practice to do evil, and so with forethought go on in the road to perdition.

debates: Whether the flesh here means the whole man by nature or only the unrenewed part of a believer.
Whether the will is the soul’s remaining friend to God or is itself depraved.
What the repetition in these verses is for.
Whether the disowning of the deed leaves guilt intact.
What accounts for the gap between willing and performing.
outliers: Wesley’s one-line gloss on the flesh contradicts the division Calvin builds out of the same phrase.
Clarke calls the will almost the only friend to God in the human soul and accuses those who read this very chapter of slandering it.
Clarke tells Xenophon’s story of Araspes and Cyrus to illustrate the ancient doctrine of two souls.
Calvin concedes that the best works of the faithful are always stained, so that no reward can be hoped unless God pardons them.
Theodoret makes the impotence a consequence of bodily mortality rather than of the will at all.

21.pericope_label: I find then a law — I delight in the law of God after the inward man — but I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind

schools.summary: Set out the choice on the difficult word: of the many ways of taking it two stand out, the first being rule or habitually repeated fact, which most commentators adopt, against which lies the objection that it gives the word an entirely different sense from the one it bears in the context or anywhere else in the apostle; the second assuming a broken construction, the sentence begun as though it would say that the Mosaic law is found unable to help and then finished in another form. Keep in any case the notion of what binds, controls and influences, even though what is meant here is not imposed by a superior as a law usually is, and identify it with the carnal and corrupt nature and the evil propensities leading a man astray. Rest the case for the regenerate reading on the verb of delight, which occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and means to rejoice with, denoting not the approbation of the understanding merely, as the earlier word for consent did, but sensible pleasure in the heart, an emotion of pleasure in contemplating the law; and add that never yet did an impenitent sinner find such emotions, so that if this expression can be applied to an unrenewed man there is hardly a mark of a pious mind that could not be. Place the inward man in the higher part of a man’s nature considered as capable of receiving divine grace, midway between the mind, which is the moral and rational faculties, and the spirit, which is that nature actually in communion with God. Then supply the philology of the conflict: a rare verb for carrying on a campaign against, and a late and vivid one for capture and slavery, so that the picture is tragic, running from sold under sin to captivity to the law of sin; complete the military figure by noting that a captive taken in war was at the disposal of the victor; and observe that Plato, Ovid, Seneca and Epictetus describe the same dual struggle between conscience and deeds.

Take the first law as the corruption of nature, known by experience and called a law because of the force with which it demands compliance with its lusts, and identify it with what the Jews call the evil imagination, whose first name among the seven they assign it is evil — well named, since it is originally and continually evil, evil in its nature and in its consequences, and the spring of all evil. Count the laws in the passage and find four: the law of God, which alone is properly so called and is the rule by which life is rightly formed; the law of the mind, meaning the prompt readiness of the faithful mind to render obedience to it; the law of unrighteousness, the dominion which iniquity exercises over the unregenerate and over the flesh of the regenerate, so called by a certain similarity, since even the laws of tyrants are called laws though not properly; and the law of the members, that is the lust in the members, named for its concord with iniquity. Deny that an unregenerate man can delight in the law, since he dislikes its commands and cannot love what threatens and curses him, and since the moralist and the Pharisee obey it externally not from love of its precepts but from fear of its threatenings and from a desire of popular esteem; only a regenerate man delights in it, as fulfilled by Christ, held forth by Christ as a rule of walk, and written on the heart by the Spirit, serving it of a ready mind under no constraint but love. Locate the other law in the members not because it has its seat there but because it uses them to fulfil its lusts. And see in this division the source of the contest between the spirit and the flesh which Augustine called the Christian struggle.

Gloss the first law as an inward constraining power flowing from the dictate of corrupt nature, and take the word to mean any strong or confirmed habit under whose influence a man generally acts, as the old lexicographer renders it; describe the state accordingly, that the will to do good is constantly at hand and the principle of rebellion equally so, but that since the one is only will and wish without power to do what is willed, sin continually prevails. Refuse to make the delight a mark of regeneration: every Jew and every unregenerate man who receives the Old Testament as revelation must acknowledge the purity and excellence and utility of its maxims, though he will find that without grace he can never act by them; and say that to make the inward man mean the regenerate part of the soul is supportable by no argument, the phrases being frequent among the purest Greek moralists for the soul or rational part of man as opposed to the body, and paralleled among the Jews, who call the flesh the inward garment and the Spirit the inward man whose garment is the body. Then draw the conflict as a siege: reason and conscience testify against sin continually, but while help is sought only from the law their remonstrances are rendered of no effect by passions which repeated gratification has hardened into habit; and the verb alludes to a city besieged and at last taken by storm, the enemy carrying on a system of warfare, laying continual siege to the soul, repeating incessantly its attacks, harassing, battering and storming the spirit and reducing the man to extreme misery. Note in passing that the delight is more than the consent spoken of earlier, and that the day of liberty draws near.

Solve the difficult verse by repunctuating it, putting a full stop after the wish to do what is right, and then supply what brevity has obscured: the law appears good, all that it recommends being approved as right and excellent, and in unison with it the man loves all good and hates its opposite, but nevertheless evil is ever at hand, that is sin, by reason of a mortal body subject to passions and appetites and through the indolence and weakness of the soul. Take the inward man to be simply the mind. Explain the captivity from the soul’s own history: sin works by the passions of the body leaping about at pleasure while the soul cannot restrain them, having fallen at first into sluggishness and cast off her own freedom and allowed herself to be subjected to them, though even while obeying she hates that servitude and approves the law that condemns it. Say that all this is laid down to show what we were before grace and what we have become since, the writer personating the character of those besieged by sin before grace appeared, so that as one in the midst of enemies, taken captive and compelled to obey and perceiving help from no other quarter, he groans bitterly and cries out. And elsewhere turn the same verse to the Incarnation, since the devil had used the flesh as an instrument against us, and by the very same weapons the victory was to be won back.

Defend the passage against its readers rather than expound it: it does not represent the apostle as one that walked after the flesh, but as one that had it greatly at heart not to walk so; and if there are those who abuse it, as they also abuse the other Scriptures, to their own destruction, serious Christians still find cause to bless God for having thus provided for their support and comfort, and we are not, because of the abuse of such as are blinded by their own lusts, to find fault with the Scripture or with any just and well warranted interpretation of it. Add that no man who is not engaged in this conflict can clearly understand the meaning of these words or rightly judge concerning this painful conflict, which led the apostle to bemoan himself as a wretched man constrained to what he abhorred; and that being unable to deliver himself he thanked God the more fervently for the way of salvation revealed through Jesus Christ, which promised him deliverance from this enemy in the end.

debates: What the word law means in the twenty-first verse.
How many distinct laws the passage names.
Whether delight in the law of God can be predicated of an unregenerate man.
What the inward man is.
Who is responsible for the captivity described in the twenty-third verse.
outliers: Barnes rests the whole regenerate reading on a verb that occurs nowhere else in the New Testament; Clarke answers that any Jew must acknowledge the law’s excellence.
Clarke denies that the inward man can mean the regenerate part of the soul, citing Greek moralists and a rabbinic parallel against it.
Calvin distinguishes four laws where the others find two.
Gill identifies the law he finds with the rabbinic evil imagination and its seven names.
Cyril uses the verse to argue the Incarnation rather than to describe the conflict.
Robertson observes that Plato, Ovid, Seneca and Epictetus describe the same dual struggle.

24.pericope_label: O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death? — I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord

schools.summary: Give the adjective its history, an old word from bearing and a callus, found only twice in the New Testament, and take over another’s phrase for the whole, a heart-rending cry from the depths of despair; settle the construction so that the order of words demands deliverance out of the body of this death; and answer the suspicion of exaggeration by recalling that the same writer described himself as chief of sinners, dealing too honestly with himself for Pharisaic complacency to live long in him. Trace the effects of the conflict rather than defining its object: it produces pain and distress, an agonising struggle that annoys the peace and renders life wretched, and it produces humility, since it is degrading to a man to be under the control of such propensities; and the mind so overwhelmed instinctively sighs for relief, asking whether the law can aid, or man, or any native strength of conscience or reason, and finding all of them tried in vain. Elsewhere make the body itself the cause of sin and therefore of death, so that the cry asks release from the whole of this mortal nature in which carnal appetite and sin and death are inextricably mingled, and hold that the triple resurrection, ethical and spiritual and physical, is needed to complete the deliverance. Take the thanksgiving as the point to which all the reasoning tended, the superiority of the gospel to the law being now triumphantly established, since what conscience could not do and the law could not do and unaided human strength could not do has been accomplished by the plan of the gospel. Mark the structure as well, the obligation to be sanctified having been proved in the preceding chapters and the possibility of it being the business of what follows. And judge the deliverance to be that of sanctification rather than of justification, a freeing from the domination of the body and the impulses of sense, effected when a man is crucified to them with Christ.

Fence the misery about before expounding it: the man is not wretched as considered in Christ, for so he is blessed with all spiritual blessings and secure from condemnation; nor with respect to his inward man, which is renewing day by day and enjoys spiritual peace; nor with regard to his future state, of whose happiness he had no doubt, knowing in whom he had believed and being persuaded nothing could separate him from the love of God; nor even chiefly on account of reproaches and persecutions, which he rather took pleasure in; but on account of the continual combat between flesh and spirit and the mass of corruption he carried about with him. Insist that the question is not asked in doubt, as unbelievers ask who do not understand that there is but one real deliverer, but is the voice of one panting and almost fainting because he does not find immediate help; and note that the word for rescue means a forcible act effected by power, showing that no ordinary exercise of divine power was needed for his liberation. Add the thanksgiving immediately, lest any think the complaint a perverse murmuring against God, since the transition from legitimate grief to discontent is easy, and it does not become the saints while examining their defects to forget what they have already received. Report the variant reading which makes the grace of God the direct answer to the question, and expound it so, that the grace of the Father communicated through Christ by the Spirit will in the end deliver from indwelling sin and all its effects; but where the context gives no strong reason, follow what the manuscripts mostly sanction and keep the received text.

Finish the account with the groans of the wounded captive, who after a useless conflict against innumerable hosts and irresistible might is wounded and taken prisoner, and whose state is made worse still by being not only encompassed by the slaughtered but chained to a dead body — in allusion to the ancient custom of certain tyrants who bound a dead body to a living man, limb to limb and face to face, and obliged him to carry it until the contagion from the putrid mass took away his life, as Virgil paints it in his account of Mezentius. Take the body of this death as this mass of sin, leading to death eternal and cleaving as close to the man as his body to his soul; observe that the struggle has now come to its height, so that finding no help in himself he begins almost unawares to pray, and that the word translated deliver implies force, without which there can be no deliverance; and note plainly that the deliverance is not wrought yet. Report the variant reading found in several excellent manuscripts, the Vulgate and some of the fathers, which gives the grace of God through our Lord Jesus Christ in place of the thanksgiving, and print the two verses accordingly as a question and its answer. Then keep the reading of the whole passage to the end: the I is the person being personated until the deliverance is wrought, the mind and conscience declaring for God while the corrupt passions still rebel, and the man now utterly weary of his bondage and upon the brink of liberty. Interweave the assertion with thanksgiving, the hymn of praise answering the voice of sorrow.

Explain the phrase narrowly, that it is called a body of death as being born subject to death, that is mortal, since the soul is immortal. Then set the deliverance in two ages: Christ alone has freed us from this bitter bondage by putting an end to death and promising immortality and a life without labour or pain, apart from warfare and sin, the full enjoyment of which we shall receive in the existence to come; while in the present we are blessed with the grace of the thrice holy Spirit, so that we not only set ourselves against the passions but by the possession of such a Helper are enabled to triumph over them. And bring forward the summary as the resolution of everything that has been said, that the same person with the mind serves the law of God and with the flesh the law of sin.

debates: What the body of this death is — the mortal body, the mass of sin, or the whole of human nature.
Whether the question is asked in doubt or in longing.
Whether the thanksgiving or the grace of God is the true reading of the answer.
Whether the deliverance spoken of is justification or sanctification.
Whether the deliverance has already been received or is still awaited.
outliers: Clarke illustrates the verse from the tyrant Mezentius in Virgil, who bound the living to the dead.
Gill lists at length all the senses in which the speaker is not wretched before allowing the one in which he is.
Ellicott requires a triple resurrection, ethical and spiritual and physical, to complete the deliverance.
Wesley alone points out that the deliverance is not yet wrought.
Clarke and Gill adopt the variant that turns the two verses into question and answer; Calvin weighs it and keeps the received text.
Robertson reads the paragraph as the hinge of the epistle’s argument about sanctification.
